description: Deep C for systems work: undefined behaviour, memory layout and ABIs, toolchain and startup, concurrency and interrupt context, Linux kernel idioms, driver programming and bare-metal embedded. For an architect who needs to read, review and reason about kernel, driver and firmware code.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.text: In C, {{c1::undefined}} behaviour means the standard imposes no requirements and the optimiser may assume it never happens; {{c2::unspecified}} means several outcomes are allowed and none is documented (e.g. argument evaluation order); {{c3::implementation-defined}} means the implementation chooses and must document it (e.g. sizeof(int), signedness of char).
notes.extra: Why it matters: in kernel and firmware code undefined behaviour (UB) becomes silent memory corruption or a security hole.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Why may if (x + 1 < x) with int x compile to false?
notes.back: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour (UB), so the optimiser assumes it never happens and the test is always false. Unsigned arithmetic, by contrast, is defined to wrap modulo 2<sup>N</sup>.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What is the portable way to detect overflow of a + b in C?
notes.back: Test before the operation, or use __builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &res), which returns true on overflow (kernel wrapper: check_add_overflow()).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What is C's integer promotion rule?
notes.back: Operands narrower than int (char, short, uint8_t, uint16_t, bitfields) become int if it can hold all their values, otherwise unsigned int.
notes.analogy: Small coins are exchanged for the standard note (int) before any arithmetic happens at the till.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: uint16_t x = 0xFFFF; uint32_t y = x * x; with 32-bit int: what goes wrong?
notes.back: Both operands promote to signed int; 0xFFFE0001 exceeds INT_MAX, so it is signed overflow (UB). Fix: (uint32_t)x * x.
notes.extra: On a 16-bit-int microcontroller unit (MCU) (AVR, MSP430) uint16_t is unsigned int: the product wraps to 1 before widening. Defined, but wrong.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: if (-1 < 1U): which branch is taken, and why?
notes.back: The false branch. With equal rank the usual arithmetic conversions make the signed operand unsigned, so -1 becomes UINT_MAX.
notes.analogy: A display that can't show minus signs: a debt of 1 appears as the biggest number it can show.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What bug class do signed lengths cause, as in int len; if (len > MAX) return -EINVAL; memcpy(dst, src, len);?
notes.back: A negative len passes the check, then converts to a huge size_t in memcpy: buffer overflow. Use size_t/u32 for lengths and build with -Wsign-compare.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Which C shift operations are undefined behaviour?
notes.back:
• count negative or ≥ the width of the promoted left operand
  • left shift of a negative value
  • left shift of a signed value whose result doesn't fit (1 << 31 with 32-bit int)

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Why is the kernel's BIT(n) defined as (1UL << (n)), and what about bits ≥ 32?
notes.back: The unsigned constant avoids shifting into the sign bit (1U << 31 is fine). 1UL << 40 is undefined behaviour (UB) on 32-bit targets: use BIT_ULL(n).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What does right-shifting a negative signed value do in C?
notes.back: Implementation-defined; an arithmetic (sign-extending) shift on every relevant application binary interface (ABI).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: uint8_t b[4]; uint64_t v = b[0] | b[1] << 8 | b[2] << 16 | b[3] << 24; Find the bug.
notes.back: b[3] promotes to signed int; if ≥ 0x80, << 24 hits the sign bit (undefined behaviour (UB), in practice negative) and conversion to uint64_t sign-extends the top 32 bits to ones. Fix: (uint32_t)b[3] << 24 or get_unaligned_le32(b).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) process(a[i]); What happens?
notes.back: i >= 0 is always true for unsigned; after 0, i-- wraps to SIZE_MAX: out-of-bounds access and an endless loop. Idiom: for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; ).
notes.extra: -Wtype-limits (in -Wextra) flags the always-true comparison.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Is converting an out-of-range value to a signed integer type undefined behaviour?
notes.back: No: implementation-defined (mainstream compilers truncate modulo 2<sup>N</sup>). Conversion to an unsigned type is always defined, modulo 2<sup>N</sup>.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What did C23 change about integer representation, and what is still undefined behaviour (UB)?
notes.back: Two's complement is mandatory (ones' complement and sign-magnitude are gone). Signed arithmetic overflow remains UB.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Which are undefined behaviour (UB): i = i++ + 1; a[i] = i++; f(i++, i++); i = i + 1;?
notes.back: The first three: the object is modified twice, or modified and read, with the side effects unsequenced. i = i + 1 is fine.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Is the order in which g() and h() run in f(g(), h()) undefined behaviour?
notes.back: No, it is unspecified: either order may happen, but each call runs as a whole.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.text: C sequence points include the end of a full expression, the operators {{c1::&&, ||, ?: and comma}}, and the point {{c2::after argument evaluation, just before a function call}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: struct sock *sk = tun->sk; if (!tun) return POLLERR; Why was this an exploitable kernel bug (CVE-2009-1897)?
notes.back: tun is dereferenced before the check, so the compiler infers it is non-NULL (else undefined behaviour (UB)) and deletes the check. With page 0 mapped by user space, the kernel used attacker-controlled data.
notes.analogy: The optimiser reasons like a detective: "you opened the door, so you must have had the key", and throws away the later key check.
notes.extra: Fixes: check before use; the kernel builds with -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks; mmap_min_addr blocks mapping page 0.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: printk("%d\n", val) with u64 val: why is it wrong?
notes.back: Variadic arguments get only the default promotions, so a format/argument mismatch is undefined behaviour (UB). On 32-bit targets the 64-bit argument also misaligns every argument after it.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.text: Kernel printk formats: u64 → {{c1::%llu/%llx}}; size_t → {{c2::%zu}}; phys_addr_t → {{c3::%pa (pass &addr)}}; dma_addr_t → {{c4::%pad}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: How do you get compile-time format checking for your own printf-like logging function?
notes.back: Annotate it with __printf(fmt_idx, first_arg_idx), the kernel's spelling of __attribute__((format(printf, ...))).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Why is if (jiffies > timeout) wrong, and what is correct?
notes.back: It breaks when the counter wraps. Use time_after(jiffies, timeout), i.e. (long)(timeout - jiffies) < 0: unsigned subtraction wraps correctly and the signed cast interprets the difference.
notes.analogy: Clock-face arithmetic: "is it after 11?" fails across midnight, but "has an hour passed since I looked?" always works.
notes.extra: Valid for intervals below half the counter range.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What is the portable bare-metal timeout idiom with a wrapping millis() counter?
notes.back: Compare elapsed time: if ((uint32_t)(millis() - start) >= timeout_ms). Never compare absolute timestamps.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What is Qm.n fixed-point format?
notes.back: An integer interpreted as value / 2n. Q15 in int16_t covers [-1, 1); Q16.16 in int32_t is a common general choice. Add and subtract are plain integer operations.
notes.analogy: Like storing money as integer cents: the decimal point is a convention you keep in your head.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: How do you multiply two Q15 numbers, and what is the trap?
notes.back: Widen to int32_t (the product is Q30), add rounding 1 << 14, shift right 15. Trap: -1 × -1 = +1 is not representable, so saturate to INT16_MAX.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: On a Cortex-M4F, why write 1.0f rather than 1.0?
notes.back: Its floating-point unit (FPU) is single-precision only; 1.0 is a double, which forces slow software double-precision arithmetic.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What bug does kmalloc(n * sizeof(*p), GFP_KERNEL) invite when n comes from user space or a device?
notes.back: The multiplication can wrap, giving an undersized buffer and then a heap overflow.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Which kernel helpers make size calculations overflow-safe?
notes.back: kmalloc_array()/kcalloc() (return NULL on overflow), struct_size()/array_size() (saturate to SIZE_MAX), and check_mul_overflow() (returns true on overflow).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: State C's strict aliasing rule.
notes.back: An object may only be accessed through its own type (or qualified/signed/unsigned variant), an aggregate containing it, or a character type. Anything else is undefined behaviour (UB), so the compiler may assume an int * and a float * never alias.
notes.analogy: The compiler treats differently typed pointers as separate bank accounts: a deposit to one can't change the other's balance, so it keeps cached balances.
notes.extra: The kernel and much firmware build with -fno-strict-aliasing; otherwise reinterpret bytes with memcpy().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Is strict aliasing's character-type exemption symmetric?
notes.back: No. Any object may be read through unsigned char *, but a char buf[] may not be read through a uint32_t *.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What are the correct ways to reinterpret a float's bits as a uint32_t, and the common wrong one?
notes.back: memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof u) (always valid, compiles to one move) or a union (valid in C, not C++). Wrong: *(uint32_t *)&f, a strict-aliasing violation.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What is an object's effective type, and what effective type does freshly allocated memory have?
notes.back: A declared object's effective type is its declared type. Allocated memory has none until written: the first store through a non-character type sets it, and rewriting can change it.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Why is reading a declared char buf[N] through a u32 * undefined behaviour (UB) even when aligned?
notes.back: Its effective type stays char, so it is a strict-aliasing violation. memcpy() out of it is always valid.
notes.extra: Custom pools built on a char array are one more reason firmware uses -fno-strict-aliasing.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What exactly does volatile guarantee?
notes.back: Every source-level read and write becomes a real load/store, in program order, never cached in a register or elided.
notes.analogy: volatile says "read the actual gauge every time; don't trust your memory of the last reading".

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What does volatile NOT give you?
notes.back: Atomicity (v++ is still load-add-store), mutual exclusion, ordering between CPUs (barriers), or cache coherency for direct memory access (DMA) buffers.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What are the legitimate uses of volatile?
notes.back: Memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) registers, variables shared with an interrupt service routine (ISR) or signal handler, and locals that must survive longjmp().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What does restrict promise, and what happens if the promise is broken?
notes.back: For the pointer's lifetime, the object is accessed only through it (or pointers derived from it), so the compiler can skip reloads and vectorise. Breaking it is undefined behaviour (UB) and never diagnosed.
notes.analogy: Telling the movers you hold the only key to the room, so they can rearrange furniture without checking whether anyone else moved it.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: memcpy() vs memmove(): what is the rule, and where does it bite?
notes.back: Overlapping buffers in memcpy are undefined behaviour (UB) (its parameters are restrict); memmove handles overlap. Shifting data within one buffer, such as dropping a consumed header, overlaps by construction.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What should you use to copy to or from a memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) region?
notes.back: memcpy_toio() / memcpy_fromio(). Plain memcpy may use access widths, unaligned accesses or instructions that device memory doesn't tolerate.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.text: Read C declarations right to left: const char *p is {{c1::a pointer to const char (can't write through p)}}; char *const p is {{c2::a const pointer to char (can't reseat p)}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: When is writing through a cast-away const undefined behaviour (UB), and what happens in practice?
notes.back: Only if the object itself was defined const. Kernel: it sits in write-protected .rodata → oops. Microcontroller: it sits in flash → write ignored or bus fault.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Does a const T * parameter guarantee the data won't change during the call?
notes.back: No. It is the callee's promise not to write through that pointer; another alias may still modify the data.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: When is C pointer arithmetic valid?
notes.back: Only within one array object (a single object counts as an array of 1) or to one past the end, which may not be dereferenced. Merely forming a pointer outside that range is undefined behaviour (UB).
notes.extra: Arithmetic on void * is a GNU extension (element size 1), used all over the kernel.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Which pointer comparisons are defined in C?
notes.back: ==/!= between any pointers; <, > and subtraction (giving ptrdiff_t) only within the same object.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: How should C code convert pointers to integers?
notes.back: Through uintptr_t; the mapping is implementation-defined. The kernel uses unsigned long.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: When does a C array NOT decay to a pointer?
notes.back: As the operand of sizeof, _Alignof, typeof or unary &, and when a string literal initialises an array.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What is sizeof(buf) inside void f(char buf[64]), and how does the kernel guard against this mistake?
notes.back: The pointer size (4 or 8): the parameter is adjusted to char *. ARRAY_SIZE() contains __must_be_array(), which breaks the build when given a pointer.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.text: In C, static at file scope gives {{c1::internal linkage}}; static at block scope gives {{c2::static storage duration (one persistent instance, which makes the function non-reentrant)}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What does -fno-common (default since GCC 10) change?
notes.back: int x; tentatively defined in two files becomes a multiple-definition link error instead of being silently merged. Put extern int x; in the header and one definition in a .c file.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Why is static inline the idiom for functions in C headers?
notes.back: C99 plain inline emits no external symbol; if the compiler doesn't inline (e.g. at -O0) the link fails unless one translation unit (TU) provides an extern inline definition. static inline gives each TU a private copy if needed.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Why prefer a static inline function over a function-like macro?
notes.back: Type checking, and each argument is evaluated exactly once.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Why wrap a multi-statement macro in do { ... } while (0)?
notes.back: It makes the macro a single statement that requires a trailing ;, so if (x) FOO(); else ... parses correctly.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What is a GNU statement expression ({ ...; v; }) used for in macros?
notes.back: Declaring temporaries and yielding a value, so each argument is evaluated once, e.g. the kernel's min() uses typeof(a) _a = (a);.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What goes wrong with #define min(a, b) ((a) < (b) ? (a) : (b))?
notes.back: An argument is evaluated twice: min(i++, j) increments twice, min(readl(reg), x) reads a read-to-clear register twice.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What do # and ## do in a C macro?
notes.back: #x turns the argument into a string literal; a##b pastes tokens, used to generate families of symbols (initcalls, register accessors, X-macros).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Why does the kernel need a two-level __stringify(x) → __stringify_1(x)?
notes.back: Operands of #/## are not macro-expanded first. The extra level expands PAGE_SIZE to 4096 before stringifying.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What is the lifetime of a compound literal like (struct pt){ .x = 1 } inside a function?
notes.back: Automatic storage until the end of the enclosing block, not just the expression. At file scope it has static storage.
notes.extra: Handy for one-off arguments: f((int[]){1, 2, 3}, 3);. Returning its address is a dangling pointer.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Name four ways to end up with a dangling pointer in C.
notes.back:
• address of an automatic variable returned or stored
  • use after free()/kfree()
  • a block-scope object or compound literal used after its block
  • realloc() moving the block while old pointers remain

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Which dangling-pointer bug is specific to interrupt- or callback-driven code?
notes.back: Handing a pointer to a stack object to something that outlives the function (timer, work item, direct memory access (DMA) transfer, queued message). The frame is reused and the callback or device writes into someone else's stack.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Why are Variable Length Arrays banned from the Linux kernel?
notes.back: Kernel stacks are small and fixed, so a VLA sized from input is a stack-overflow primitive; VLAs are also slower and defeat stack-depth analysis. VLA-free since 4.20 (-Wvla); use a fixed worst case or kmalloc().
notes.extra: On a microcontroller unit (MCU) without memory management unit (MMU) it is worse: no guard page, so overflow silently corrupts .bss or the heap.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: How do you check an invariant at compile time in C11 and in the kernel?
notes.back: C11: _Static_assert(expr, "msg") / static_assert. Kernel: also BUILD_BUG_ON(cond), which breaks the build when cond is true.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: What is a typical driver use of static_assert?
notes.back: Pinning hardware or application binary interface (ABI) layouts so refactors can't break them: static_assert(sizeof(struct foo_desc) == 16); and static_assert(offsetof(struct foo_regs, irq_status) == 0x20);

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: How does kernel C express polymorphism?
notes.back: A const struct of function pointers (an ops table such as struct file_operations) filled with designated initialisers; objects point to it. Unset members are NULL and the core checks them or uses a default.
notes.analogy: An ops table is a C++ vtable you write by hand.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Why are kernel ops tables declared const?
notes.back: They land in read-only memory, so an attacker with a write primitive can't overwrite a function pointer to hijack control flow.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Sizes of struct a { char c1; int i; char c2; } and struct b { int i; char c1; char c2; } on a typical application binary interface (ABI)?
notes.back: a = 12 (1 + 3 pad + 4 + 1 + 3 tail pad); b = 8 (4 + 1 + 1 + 2 tail pad). Ordering members from largest to smallest alignment minimises padding.
notes.analogy: Parking cars of different widths in bays that must start on a lane marker: gaps appear unless you park the wide ones first.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Which layout rules produce struct padding in C?
notes.back: Each member sits at a multiple of its own alignment; the struct's alignment is that of its strictest member; tail padding makes sizeof a multiple of it so arrays stay aligned.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Which tool shows holes and cache-line boundaries in kernel structs?
notes.back: pahole, which reads DWARF debug info and prints offsets, holes and cache-line boundaries.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What does __attribute__((packed)) do?
notes.back: Removes padding and sets the struct's alignment to 1, so members may be unaligned. Access through the struct is safe (the compiler emits byte-wise or unaligned-capable code), just slower.
notes.extra: Use __packed only for layouts dictated by hardware or a protocol.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What is the hazard of taking &p->field of a packed struct?
notes.back: The resulting plain u32 * loses the "may be unaligned" information, so dereferencing it can fault on strict-alignment CPUs (-Waddress-of-packed-member).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: How does unaligned access behave on x86, Cortex-M0 and Cortex-M3/M4, and what does kernel code use?
notes.back: x86: fine. Cortex-M0: always faults. Cortex-M3/M4: configurable trap. Kernel: get_unaligned(), put_unaligned(), get_unaligned_le32().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why is struct hdr *h = (struct hdr *)buf; len = h->length; a fragile way to parse a packet?
notes.back: Four independent problems: alignment of buf, strict aliasing, the wire's endianness, and compiler padding that may not match the wire layout.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What is the robust way to read a field from a byte buffer in kernel C?
notes.back: Assemble it from bytes with get_unaligned_be16(buf + 2), or memcpy() into a local struct with explicitly sized, endian-annotated members and convert.
notes.extra: The kernel does cast, but only onto __packed structs with __be16/__le32 members, built with -fno-strict-aliasing.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: How does kernel code convert endianness?
notes.back: cpu_to_le32(), le32_to_cpu(), cpu_to_be16()... which compile to nothing when the CPU already matches. Convert exactly once at the device or wire boundary.
notes.analogy: Dates written YYYY-MM-DD vs DD-MM-YYYY: same digits, different order; you convert once at the border.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: How are endianness mistakes caught at build time in the kernel?
notes.back: __le32, __be16... are __bitwise types; sparse (make C=1) reports mixing them with plain integers or each other without a conversion.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: Byte order: network byte order is {{c1::big-endian}}; Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI) and USB are {{c2::little-endian}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why are C bitfields avoided for hardware registers and wire formats?
notes.back: Bit order, straddling, storage-unit type and signedness are implementation-defined; the access width isn't guaranteed; and each assignment is a non-atomic read-modify-write that can clobber write-1-to-clear bits.
notes.extra: Use masks and shifts: GENMASK(), FIELD_PREP(), FIELD_GET().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Two contexts each write a different bitfield of the same struct. Why can they still race?
notes.back: Adjacent bitfields share a storage unit and each write is a read-modify-write of the whole unit, so one write can undo the other.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What is the underlying type of a C enum?
notes.back: Enumeration constants have type int; the enum type itself is an implementation-defined integer type wide enough for all its values.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why is -fshort-enums an application binary interface (ABI) hazard?
notes.back: It picks the smallest type. Bare-metal ARM toolchains often use variable-size enums while Linux ABIs use int, so mixing objects silently changes struct layouts and argument sizes (linker warns about "variable-size enums").
notes.extra: Never put an enum in a wire format or user-space ABI struct; use a fixed-width integer.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Is plain char signed?
notes.back: Implementation-defined: signed on x86, unsigned on ARM, PowerPC and reduced instruction set computer (RISC)-V. Since Linux 6.2 the kernel builds with -funsigned-char everywhere.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What bugs come from plain char signedness?
notes.back: c < 0 or c == EOF tests, negative array indices, and sign extension of bytes ≥ 0x80: works on x86, breaks on ARM. Use u8 for bytes, char only for text.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: C data models: ILP32 has {{c1::32-bit int, long and pointer}}; LP64 has {{c2::64-bit long and pointer with a 32-bit int}} (Linux, macOS); LLP64 has {{c3::only long long and pointer at 64 bits, long stays 32}} (Windows).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Which size invariant does Linux kernel code rely on?
notes.back: sizeof(long) == sizeof(void *), so unsigned long is the pointer-sized integer. Use u8..u64 for fixed layouts and __u32 etc. in uapi headers.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: {{c1::offsetof(type, member)}} gives a member's byte offset (the basis of container_of); {{c2::_Alignof(type)}} gives the required alignment; {{c3::_Alignas(n)}} (kernel __aligned(n)) raises an object's alignment.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Where do drivers need explicit alignment?
notes.back: Direct memory access (DMA) descriptors that hardware requires on 8/16/64-byte boundaries, buffers aligned to the cache line for cache maintenance, and hot per-CPU data on separate cache lines.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: A driver fills a stack struct member by member, then copy_to_user()s it. What is the vulnerability?
notes.back: Padding bytes and unassigned members still hold stale kernel stack contents: an information leak that can defeat kernel address space layout randomization (KASLR) or expose keys.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why doesn't struct s x = {0}; reliably fix a padding leak, and what does?
notes.back: Initialisers zero the members; padding isn't guaranteed zero. memset(&x, 0, sizeof(x)) first, or design the struct with no implicit padding (explicit reserved fields).
notes.extra: Hardening: CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL_ZERO (-ftrivial-auto-var-init=zero).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What is a C99 flexible array member, and how does the kernel allocate one safely?
notes.back: u8 data[]; as the last member; sizeof excludes it. Allocate with kmalloc(struct_size(m, data, n), GFP_KERNEL), which saturates to SIZE_MAX on overflow so the allocation fails instead of being too small.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why did the kernel purge [0] and [1] trailing arrays?
notes.back: They defeat compiler bounds checking (-fstrict-flex-arrays=3, FORTIFY_SOURCE, __counted_by()), and [1] makes sizeof one element too big.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: x86-64 System V application binary interface (ABI): integer arguments in {{c1::rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9}}; return value in {{c2::rax}}; callee-saved registers {{c3::rbx, rbp, r12–r15}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What is the x86-64 red zone, and why does the kernel build with -mno-red-zone?
notes.back: 128 bytes below rsp that a leaf function may use without moving rsp. In the kernel, interrupts push their frame onto the same stack and would overwrite it.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: 32-bit ARM Arm Architecture Procedure Call Standard (AAPCS): arguments and return value in {{c1::r0–r3}}; callee-saved {{c2::r4–r11}}; stack aligned to {{c3::8 bytes}} at public interfaces.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: How large is a Linux kernel stack, and can it grow?
notes.back: Fixed per thread: 16 KiB on x86-64 and arm64, 8 KiB on 32-bit ARM. It never grows.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Which coding rules follow from the small, fixed kernel stack?
notes.back: No large locals (use kmalloc()), no unbounded recursion, no variable-length arrays (VLAs) or alloca(). -Wframe-larger-than= and scripts/checkstack.pl find offenders.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What does CONFIG_VMAP_STACK change?
notes.back: Kernel stacks live in vmalloc space with guard pages, so an overflow faults immediately; side effect: stack memory can't be used for direct memory access (DMA).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: kmalloc() vs vmalloc()?
notes.back: kmalloc: slab-backed, physically contiguous, fast; for small objects (KiB). vmalloc: only virtually contiguous; for large buffers; may sleep; not directly usable for direct memory access (DMA).
notes.analogy: kmalloc: adjacent seats in one row. vmalloc: seats scattered around the theatre, with a seating map that makes them look adjacent.
notes.extra: Every allocation can fail: always check for NULL.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: Kernel allocators: {{c1::kvmalloc()}} tries kmalloc and falls back to vmalloc (free with kvfree()); {{c2::kmem_cache_create()}} creates a slab cache for many same-sized objects; {{c3::dma_alloc_coherent()}} allocates a buffer shared with a device.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: Allocation flags: {{c1::GFP_KERNEL}} may sleep to reclaim memory (process context, no spinlock held); {{c2::GFP_ATOMIC}} never sleeps and may dip into reserves (interrupt request (IRQ) handlers, under spinlocks); {{c3::GFP_NOWAIT}} never sleeps and gets no reserves.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What happens if you allocate with GFP_KERNEL in atomic context, and what is the better design?
notes.back: "BUG: sleeping function called from invalid context" (with DEBUG_ATOMIC_SLEEP) or a deadlock. Better: allocate in probe() or process context and only use the memory in the interrupt request (IRQ) path.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: Driver addresses: a {{c1::kernel virtual address (void *)}} is what the CPU dereferences; a {{c2::physical address (phys_addr_t)}} must be mapped first (ioremap(), memremap()); a {{c3::DMA/bus address (dma_addr_t)}} is what the device puts on the bus and may differ because of an input-output memory management unit (IOMMU).
notes.analogy: One building, three addresses: the street address you use (virtual), the land-registry plot number (physical), and the courier company's own code for it (DMA address via the IOMMU).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: When is virt_to_phys() valid?
notes.back: Only for the kernel's linear mapping (kmalloc memory), not vmalloc, stack or ioremap addresses. Devices may only be given addresses from the direct memory access (DMA) mapping API.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why may a driver not dereference a user-space pointer directly?
notes.back: It may be invalid or unmapped (the access must fault safely), or point into kernel memory (confused deputy). Supervisor mode access prevention (SMAP) (x86) and privileged access never (PAN) (ARM) make a direct access fault anyway.
notes.extra: The __user annotation lets sparse flag direct dereferences.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What does copy_from_user() return, and how do you handle it?
notes.back: The number of bytes not copied; non-zero means return -EFAULT. For single scalars use get_user()/put_user().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What is a double-fetch (TOCTOU) bug in an ioctl handler?
notes.back: The handler reads uarg->len from user memory to validate it, then fetches it again to use it; another thread changes it in between. Rule: copy the whole argument in once, then validate and use only the kernel copy.
notes.analogy: Checking a passenger's ticket, then letting them swap it for another before boarding.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What is false sharing?
notes.back: Two CPUs write different variables that share one cache line (typically 64 B). Each write invalidates the other's copy, so the line ping-pongs and throughput collapses despite no logical sharing.
notes.analogy: Two people editing different paragraphs of one page that only one of them may hold at a time.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What are the kernel remedies for false sharing?
notes.back: ____cacheline_aligned_in_smp on hot fields or structs, separating read-mostly (__read_mostly) from write-hot fields, and per-CPU counters.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Memory-mapped I/O vs port I/O?
notes.back: MMIO: registers in the physical address space, mapped with ioremap() and accessed with readl()/writel(); universal on ARM, reduced instruction set computer (RISC)-V and Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe). Port I/O: a separate x86 address space (inb()/outb()) for legacy devices.
notes.extra: ioread32()/iowrite32() with pci_iomap() work for both.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why can't a Linux driver just cast a physical register address to a pointer?
notes.back: The address must be mapped into kernel virtual space, and device mappings need uncached device-memory attributes, which ioremap() sets up.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why is floating point forbidden in Linux kernel code?
notes.back: On kernel entry only integer registers are saved; the floating-point unit (FPU)/vector state still belongs to the interrupted user task, so using it would corrupt user state. Saving it on every entry costs too much.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: What is the escape hatch for floating-point unit (FPU)/single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) use in the kernel?
notes.back: kernel_fpu_begin()/kernel_fpu_end() on x86, kernel_neon_begin() on ARM: preemption off, no sleeping. Used by crypto and redundant array of independent disks (RAID) code; otherwise use fixed point.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why must driver code use PAGE_SIZE rather than hard-coding 4096?
notes.back: Page size is a build-time choice: arm64 supports 4, 16 and 64 KiB, PowerPC often uses 64 KiB. Hard-coded 4096 breaks mmap handlers, scatter-gather lists and ring sizing.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.text: PAGE_SIZE = {{c1::1UL << PAGE_SHIFT}}; PAGE_MASK = {{c2::~(PAGE_SIZE - 1)}}; ALIGN(x, a) for power-of-two a = {{c3::(x + a - 1) & ~(a - 1)}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.text: C build stages: preprocess (gcc -E) produces {{c1::.i, text with macros and includes expanded}}; compile (-S) produces {{c2::.s, assembly}}; assemble (-c) produces {{c3::an Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) .o object}}; link (ld) {{c4::resolves symbols, applies relocations and places sections}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What is a translation unit, and what does it imply for optimisation?
notes.back: One .c file plus all its headers after preprocessing. The compiler sees one TU at a time; cross-file knowledge comes only from declarations unless Link Time Optimisation is enabled.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: How does firmware get from an Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) file to a flashable image?
notes.back: objcopy -O binary (or -O ihex) strips the ELF metadata down to raw bytes.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Hosted vs freestanding C implementation?
notes.back: Hosted: full standard library, program starts at main(). Freestanding (kernels, bare metal): only type/macro headers are guaranteed (stddef.h, stdint.h, limits.h, stdarg.h, stdbool.h...), and the entry point is implementation-defined.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Under -ffreestanding -nostdlib, which functions must you still provide, and why?
notes.back: memcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp: compilers emit calls for struct copies and large initialisers. Also libgcc helpers such as __aeabi_uldivmod for 64-bit division on 32-bit ARM.
notes.extra: The kernel provides its own and uses do_div()/div_u64() for 64-bit division.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.text: Image sections: {{c1::.text}} holds code; {{c2::.rodata}} const objects and string literals; {{c3::.data}} initialised writable objects; {{c4::.bss}} zero-initialised objects, taking no space in the image.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Firmware: what are the LMA and VMA of .data, and who bridges them?
notes.back: Virtual memory address (VMA): the RAM address where it lives at run time. Load memory address (LMA): the flash address where its initial values are stored. Startup code copies LMA → VMA (and zeroes .bss) before main(); linker script > RAM AT > FLASH.
notes.analogy: Furniture shipped in a moving van (flash) must be unpacked into the house (RAM) before anyone lives there.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: On Cortex-M reset, what does the hardware itself load from the vector table?
notes.back: Word 0 into the Main Stack Pointer (MSP), word 1 into the program counter (PC) (the reset handler). The table is at address 0 by default.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What does a Cortex-M Reset_Handler do before main()?
notes.back: Copies .data from flash to RAM, zeroes .bss, calls SystemInit() (clocks, flash wait states, floating-point unit (FPU), VTOR), runs constructors (__libc_init_array), then calls main().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Why can a Cortex-M reset handler be written in C, and what must it avoid?
notes.back: C fundamentally needs only a valid stack pointer, which the hardware loads. It must not touch globals until .data and .bss are initialised.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: How should C code use a linker-script symbol such as _sbss?
notes.back: It is an address with no storage behind it: declare extern uint32_t _sbss; (or extern char _sbss[];) and use only its address. Reading its value fetches whatever is stored there.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What is a weak symbol?
notes.back: A definition (__attribute__((weak)), kernel __weak) that any strong definition of the same name overrides at link time, without a duplicate-symbol error.
notes.analogy: The default ringtone: any ringtone you pick replaces it, and if you pick none it still plays.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: How do Cortex-M startup files use weak symbols, and what is the trap?
notes.back: Every interrupt service routine (ISR) name is a weak alias of Default_Handler (an infinite loop); defining USART1_IRQHandler overrides it. Misspell the name and it still links: the interrupt request (IRQ) lands in Default_Handler and the system appears to hang.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What do -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wl,--gc-sections do?
notes.back: Put every function and object in its own section, then let the linker drop sections unreachable from the entry point: large flash savings with vendor libraries.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Why does the vector table need KEEP() in the linker script?
notes.back: No C code references it; only the hardware reads it. Without KEEP(*(.isr_vector)) it is garbage-collected and the chip won't boot. Same for tables found only by section iteration (initcalls).
notes.analogy: A cleaner throws out everything nobody mentions; the vector table is only read by the hardware, so it must be on the explicit keep list.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What does __attribute__((section("name"))) enable when combined with linker start/end symbols?
notes.back: An array with no central registry: each file drops entries into the section and code iterates from start to end symbol (initcalls, shell command tables, driver registries).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What do __init/__initdata do, and what bug do they invite?
notes.back: Put code/data in .init.* sections freed after boot. Calling an __init function later is a use-after-free; modpost reports it as a section mismatch.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: How does module_init(fn) work for built-in code vs a loadable module?
notes.back: Built in: fn goes into a device-level .initcall section, run by do_initcalls() in level order. Loadable: fn is aliased to init_module and called at load.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Which C dialect does the Linux kernel build with?
notes.back: -std=gnu11 (since 5.18; previously gnu89), using GNU extensions freely: typeof, statement expressions, __attribute__, case ranges, void * arithmetic.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.text: Kernel flags that define away undefined behaviour (UB): {{c1::-fno-strict-aliasing}} (type punning allowed), {{c2::-fno-strict-overflow}} (signed and pointer wrap defined), {{c3::-fno-delete-null-pointer-checks}} (NULL tests survive a prior dereference).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Why can't the Linux kernel be built at -O0?
notes.back: It relies on inlining and dead-code elimination, e.g. IS_ENABLED() branches, BUILD_BUG_ON() and __always_inline helpers.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What do likely()/unlikely() do?
notes.back: __builtin_expect hints telling the compiler which branch to lay out as fall-through, keeping hot code contiguous. They affect code layout, not the CPU's dynamic branch predictor.
notes.analogy: Arranging a kitchen so the everyday tools sit on the counter and the rare ones in the back cupboard.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: When should a driver use unlikely()?
notes.back: Only for truly skewed conditions in hot paths, such as error checks; a wrong hint is worse than none. IS_ERR() already contains it.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.text: Binary tools: nm {{c1::lists symbols (T text, D data, B bss, U undefined, W weak)}}; objdump -d {{c2::disassembles}}; readelf {{c3::shows sections, segments and relocations}}; size {{c4::prints text/data/bss totals}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: From size output, how do you estimate a microcontroller unit (MCU)'s flash and static RAM use?
notes.back: Flash ≈ text + data (initial values are stored in flash). Static RAM ≈ data + bss.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What does a linker map file (-Wl,-Map=out.map) tell you?
notes.back: Where every input section of every object landed, its size, and why it was pulled in: the tool for finding what eats flash.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What kind of file is a .ko, and what does loading it involve?
notes.back: A relocatable (not fully linked) Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) object. The loader copies its sections, resolves undefined symbols against the kernel's exports, applies relocations, checks vermagic/modversions, and runs its init function.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: EXPORT_SYMBOL vs EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL?
notes.back: Only exported symbols are visible to modules; _GPL ones only to modules with a GNU General Public License (GPL)-compatible MODULE_LICENSE. A missing export shows as "Unknown symbol in module".

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What is sparse?
notes.back: A semantic checker for kernel C (make C=1) that turns annotations into extra type-system checks; in a normal compile the annotations expand to nothing.
notes.analogy: Coloured labels on pipes (user, iomem, little-endian) that an inspector checks; the pipes themselves are unchanged.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.text: sparse annotations: {{c1::__user}} marks a user-space pointer (no direct dereference); {{c2::__iomem}} a memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) cookie (accessors only); {{c3::__bitwise}} types such as __le32 can't mix without conversion; {{c4::__acquires/__releases}} check lock balance.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: How do you cross-compile the Linux kernel for arm64?
notes.back: make ARCH=arm64 CROSS_COMPILE=aarch64-linux-gnu- defconfig Image modules dtbs

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: arm-none-eabi- vs aarch64-linux-gnu- toolchains?
notes.back: none-eabi: no OS, bare-metal Embedded Application Binary Interface (EABI), ships newlib; for microcontroller unit (MCU) firmware. linux-gnu: targets Linux with glibc; for user space and, by convention, the kernel.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: How do you make printf() work on a bare-metal newlib target?
notes.back: Retarget it: implement _write() to push bytes to an universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART) (plus _sbrk() etc. as needed). --specs=nosys.specs supplies dummies; --specs=nano.specs selects newlib-nano.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What does printf() cost on a microcontroller?
notes.back: Tens of KiB of flash with float formatting, hundreds of bytes of stack, maybe heap, not reentrant, and it blocks on the universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter (UART). Never call it from an interrupt service routine (ISR).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Why does an empty for delay loop vanish at -O2, and what should you use instead?
notes.back: It has no observable side effect, so it is removed; volatile keeps it but timing still depends on compiler, flags and clock. Use a hardware timer/SysTick, the data watchpoint and trace (DWT) cycle counter, or kernel udelay()/usleep_range().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Code works at -O0 but fails at -O2. What are the usual causes?
notes.back: A missing volatile, a data race, or undefined behaviour that the optimiser now exploits.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Why does the kernel prefer if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_FOO)) over #ifdef inside functions?
notes.back: IS_ENABLED() is a constant 1/0 (true for =y and =m), so both branches are parsed and type-checked in every configuration before the dead one is eliminated: rarely built code can't bit-rot.
notes.analogy: Proofreading every chapter, even the ones that won't be printed in this edition, so none of them rots.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What does IS_ENABLED()-style code need from headers, and where is #ifdef still required?
notes.back: Declarations used in the dead branch must stay visible (static inline stubs when the option is off). #ifdef remains for struct members and whole function definitions.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.text: Kernel attributes: {{c1::__must_check}} warns when a caller ignores the return value; {{c2::__maybe_unused}} silences unused warnings (e.g. Power management (PM) callbacks without CONFIG_PM); {{c3::__cold}} marks rarely run code, optimised for size and placed away from hot code; {{c4::fallthrough;}} marks an intentional switch fall-through.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: When do kernel developers use __always_inline vs noinline?
notes.back: __always_inline where correctness depends on inlining (constant propagation, no-instrumentation code); noinline to keep a separate stack frame or symbol, e.g. for tracing or stack usage.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Which tool checks Linux kernel coding style in a patch?
notes.back: scripts/checkpatch.pl (--strict for more checks); semantic checks come from sparse and W=1 builds.
notes.extra: Low-signal style rules (8-column tabs, line length, brace placement) were dropped from this deck.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What is the kernel coding-style rule on typedefs for structs?
notes.back: Don't: write struct foo. Exceptions are opaque or architecture-varying types (pte_t) and u8..u64.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is a data race in C11 terms, and what is its status?
notes.back: Two accesses to the same object from different threads, at least one a write, not both atomic and with no synchronisation. It is undefined behaviour.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What practical effects can a data race have?
notes.back: Torn reads and writes, a value re-loaded halfway through a computation, stores invented or merged by the compiler, stale values kept in registers.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: An interrupt service routine (ISR) and the main loop share a variable on a single-core microcontroller unit (MCU). Can they race?
notes.back: Yes: concurrency without parallelism. The ISR can run between any two instructions of the main loop.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: How does Kernel Concurrency Sanitizer (KCSAN) detect data races?
notes.back: It sets watchpoints on sampled memory accesses and reports concurrent conflicting accesses that aren't marked (READ_ONCE, atomics) or protected by locks.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why does kernel documentation call volatile "considered harmful"?
notes.back: Shared data is protected by locks, atomics or read-copy-update (RCU), which already force correct accesses. volatile on a declaration pessimises every access and hides the real concurrency design.
notes.extra: Accepted exceptions: jiffies and some device-modified memory.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.text: Kernel replacements for volatile: memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) uses {{c1::readl()/writel() on __iomem pointers}}; a single lockless access uses {{c2::READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE()}}; busy-wait loops use {{c3::cpu_relax()}}; counters use {{c4::atomic_t/refcount_t}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What do READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() do?
notes.back: Access the variable through a volatile lvalue so exactly one full-width load or store is emitted at that point, and document (to readers and Kernel Concurrency Sanitizer (KCSAN)) that the access is deliberately lockless.
notes.analogy: Taking one photo of a changing display instead of glancing twice and stitching the halves together.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.text: READ_ONCE/WRITE_ONCE prevent {{c1::refetching}} (one load compiled as two, the second maybe NULL), {{c2::tearing}} (one access split into smaller ones), {{c3::invented stores}} (the variable used as scratch space), and {{c4::fusing}} of repeated loads in a polling loop.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What do READ_ONCE/WRITE_ONCE NOT provide?
notes.back: Atomic read-modify-write, or ordering between CPUs; those need atomics or memory barriers.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: barrier() vs mb()/smp_mb()?
notes.back: barrier(): compiler-only; stops the optimiser moving accesses across it, emits no instruction. mb()/rmb()/wmb(): CPU barriers ordering accesses as seen by other CPUs or devices; smp_* variants reduce to barrier() on uniprocessor builds.
notes.analogy: A barrier is a "no overtaking" sign: accesses before it may not be reordered past accesses after it.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: You port lockless code from x86 to ARM and it breaks. What differs about memory ordering, and what does smp_wmb() compile to on each?
notes.back: x86 (TSO) only reorders a store followed by a load, so smp_rmb()/smp_wmb() are compiler barriers and smp_mb() a locked instruction. ARM, PowerPC and reduced instruction set computer (RISC)-V are weakly ordered: all emit real instructions (dmb/dsb).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why do most drivers never write explicit memory barriers?
notes.back: Locks, atomics and writel() already contain them. Explicit barriers appear in lockless rings shared with hardware or other CPUs.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why does count++ on a plain (even volatile) int lose updates under concurrency?
notes.back: It is load, add, store: two contexts interleave and one increment overwrites the other.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: atomic_t vs refcount_t?
notes.back: atomic_t: counters, flags, cmpxchg state machines. refcount_t: object lifetimes; saturates instead of wrapping and warns on increment-from-zero/underflow, turning use-after-free bugs into a leak plus a warning.
notes.extra: The kernel doesn't use C11 _Atomic; it has per-architecture implementations.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: set_bit() vs __set_bit()?
notes.back: set_bit() is atomic; the double-underscore form is non-atomic, for when you already have exclusion.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What happens with C11 _Atomic on a Cortex-M0?
notes.back: ARMv6-M lacks the LDREX/STREX exclusives, so the compiler calls __atomic_* library routines, which on bare metal are often missing (link error) or lock-based.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is the usual single-core alternative to atomics on a Cortex-M0, and its key detail?
notes.back: A short critical section: save PRIMASK, __disable_irq(), update, then restore PRIMASK rather than blindly re-enabling, so sections nest correctly.
notes.extra:
uint32_t m = __get_PRIMASK();
__disable_irq();
counter++;
__set_PRIMASK(m);

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Kernel spinlock vs mutex: what are the context rules?
notes.back: Mutex: a contended caller sleeps; process context only; the holder may sleep. Spinlock: busy-waits with preemption off; any context; the holder must not sleep (no GFP_KERNEL, copy_from_user(), msleep(), mutex_lock()).
notes.analogy: Spinlock: standing at the phone booth tapping your foot. Mutex: leaving your number and napping until called back.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: When is spin_lock_irqsave() required?
notes.back: When the lock is also taken in an interrupt request (IRQ) handler. Otherwise the IRQ can arrive on the same CPU while process context holds the lock and spin forever: self-deadlock. spin_lock_bh() suffices against softirqs.
notes.analogy: You hold the only key to a room, an interrupt sends you to that same room, and you wait at the door for yourself forever.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What happens to spinlock_t under PREEMPT_RT?
notes.back: It becomes a sleeping, rt_mutex-based lock; raw_spinlock_t remains a true spinlock.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Which kernel execution contexts may sleep?
notes.back: Only process context (syscalls, kernel threads, workqueues, threaded interrupt request (IRQ) handlers), and only with no spinlock held and preemption/IRQs enabled. Softirqs, tasklets, timer callbacks, hard IRQs and non-maskable interrupts (NMIs) may not.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: How does sleeping in atomic context show up, and how do you catch rare cases?
notes.back: "BUG: scheduling while atomic" or "sleeping function called from invalid context". Annotate functions that may sleep with might_sleep() so misuse is caught even when the sleep rarely happens.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is RCU at the API level?
notes.back: Readers take no locks (rcu_read_lock() just marks a section); updaters publish a new version and free the old one only after a grace period, once all pre-existing readers have finished. Best for read-mostly data.
notes.analogy: Updating a restaurant menu: hand out the new menus, but shred the old ones only after every diner who was reading one has finished.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What do rcu_assign_pointer() and rcu_dereference() guarantee at the C level?
notes.back: rcu_assign_pointer(): the object's initialisation is visible before the pointer is published. rcu_dereference(): the pointer is fetched exactly once.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: How does a read-copy-update (RCU) updater free the old version?
notes.back: synchronize_rcu() (waits for a grace period) followed by kfree(old), or asynchronously with kfree_rcu(old, rcu_head_field).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What are kernel per-CPU variables for?
notes.back: DEFINE_PER_CPU() gives one instance per CPU: no locking and no cache-line bouncing. Typical for statistics and per-CPU queues.
notes.analogy: Every cashier gets their own till instead of everyone fighting over one cash drawer.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why must preemption be considered when using per-CPU variables?
notes.back: A task preempted and migrated between computing the per-CPU address and using it updates another CPU's copy. Use this_cpu_inc() (one preemption-safe op) or get_cpu_var()/put_cpu_var().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is an ABBA deadlock, and what rule prevents it?
notes.back: Thread 1 takes A then B, thread 2 takes B then A; each holds what the other needs. Rule: define a global acquisition order for locks that nest.
notes.analogy: Two diners each grab one chopstick and wait forever for the other's.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: How does lockdep find deadlocks before they happen?
notes.back: It records the order in which lock classes are taken and reports the first inverse order observed, even if no deadlock occurred; it also catches interrupt request (IRQ)-safety violations and sleeping under spinlocks (CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING).
notes.analogy: A building inspector who flags a fire risk from the wiring plan, before anything has ever caught fire.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: How does a driver put a reader to sleep until the hardware has data?
notes.back: wait_event_interruptible(dev->wq, dev->data_ready) in read(); the interrupt request (IRQ) handler sets the flag and calls wake_up_interruptible(&dev->wq). A non-zero return (-ERESTARTSYS) means a signal arrived.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why is the condition an argument of wait_event() rather than checked beforehand?
notes.back: The macro checks it, marks the task sleeping, checks again, then schedules: this closes the lost-wakeup window. It also re-checks after every (possibly spurious) wake-up.
notes.analogy: Checking the mailbox once more after lying down but before closing your eyes.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: When should a driver use struct completion instead of a wait queue?
notes.back: For a one-shot "operation finished" event: wait_for_completion_timeout() on one side, complete() on the other.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: 8-bit AVR: a volatile uint32_t tick counter is incremented in an interrupt service routine (ISR) and read in main(). What is still wrong?
notes.back: The read takes four byte loads and the ISR can fire between them: a torn read (0x0000FFFF → 0x00010000 may read as 0x0001FFFF). volatile doesn't make it atomic.
notes.analogy: Reading a mechanical odometer while it rolls from 0999 to 1000 digit by digit: you may see 1999.
notes.extra: Same with a 64-bit variable on a 32-bit Cortex-M.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: How do you fix torn reads of a wide shared variable on bare metal?
notes.back: Read it inside a critical section (save interrupt request (IRQ) state, disable, copy, restore), or read it repeatedly until two consecutive reads agree.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why does a single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer need no lock?
notes.back: Each index is written by exactly one side (producer: head, consumer: tail) and only read by the other. Indices must be native-word sized so reads aren't torn.
notes.extra: Kernel equivalent: kfifo.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why size a single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer as a power of two with free-running indices?
notes.back: idx & (N - 1) replaces modulo, and unsigned wrap keeps head - tail correct, so all N slots are usable.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer: which ordering rule applies, and what is needed on multicore?
notes.back: Write the data before advancing the index. On multicore, add memory barriers between the two (kfifo contains them).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What is priority inversion?
notes.back: Low-priority L holds a mutex that high-priority H needs; medium-priority M preempts L, so H effectively waits for M without bound (the Mars Pathfinder resets).
notes.analogy: An ambulance stuck behind a slow car while other traffic keeps cutting in front of the slow car; priority inheritance gives the slow car a siren.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: How do FreeRTOS and Linux handle priority inversion?
notes.back: Priority inheritance: L runs at H's priority while H waits. FreeRTOS mutexes do it (binary semaphores don't, so don't use them for mutual exclusion); Linux has rt_mutex and PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Reentrant vs thread-safe?
notes.back: Thread-safe: correct under concurrent calls from several threads, often via a lock. Reentrant: correct when interrupted and re-entered on the same thread, which requires no static state and no non-recursive locks.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why is a lock-based thread-safe function such as malloc() unsafe to call from an interrupt service routine (ISR)?
notes.back: If the ISR interrupts the lock holder and calls it, it waits for a lock the interrupted code can never release: deadlock. Hence FreeRTOS's separate ...FromISR() APIs.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: How does a seqlock work?
notes.back: The writer increments a sequence counter before and after updating (odd = update in progress). Readers take no lock: read the counter, read the data, retry if it was odd or changed.
notes.analogy: Reading a scoreboard: check the version number, read the scores, check again; if the number changed mid-read, read again.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: When is a seqlock a good fit, and what is its limitation?
notes.back: Small, very frequently read, rarely written data such as kernel timekeeping; writers never wait for readers. Readers must not follow pointers in the data, which may be half-updated.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What does container_of(ptr, type, member) compute?
notes.back: The enclosing struct from a pointer to one of its members: (type *)((char *)ptr - offsetof(type, member)). The real macro also checks that the types match.
notes.analogy: Finding the whole car from its licence plate, because you know exactly where on the car the plate is bolted.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Why is the kernel built around container_of()?
notes.back: It enables intrusive data structures and C-style inheritance: generic code handles the embedded list_head, kref, work_struct or device, and the driver recovers its own struct in callbacks. No extra allocation or void * context.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Describe the structure of the kernel's struct list_head. What does it imply for an empty list and for how you embed it?
notes.back: It is intrusive, circular and doubly linked: the node is embedded in your struct, and the head is a node too, so an empty list points to itself and no NULL checks are needed.
notes.extra: One object can sit on several lists by embedding several nodes. Locking is the caller's job.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Which iterator must you use when deleting entries while traversing a kernel list?
notes.back: list_for_each_entry_safe(pos, tmp, head, member), which caches the next element before the body runs.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What does list_del() do to the removed node's pointers, and why?
notes.back: Poisons them (LIST_POISON1/2) so a stale use faults at a recognisable address.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How do ERR_PTR()/IS_ERR()/PTR_ERR() encode errors in pointers?
notes.back: The top 4095 addresses are never valid kernel pointers, so a negative errno is stored as a pointer value; IS_ERR(p) tests (unsigned long)p >= (unsigned long)-MAX_ERRNO.
notes.analogy: Using floor numbers the building doesn't have as error codes: no real address can ever collide with them.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What is the classic mistake with ERR_PTR-returning functions?
notes.back: Testing if (!p). A function returns either NULL or an ERR_PTR on failure (check its docs), and IS_ERR(NULL) is false.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What are the rules of the kernel's goto-based error unwinding?
notes.back: Release in exact reverse order of acquisition; name labels after what they undo; only jump forward; remove() performs the full sequence.
notes.analogy: Leaving a multi-storey car park: you drive down through the levels in the reverse order you drove up.
notes.extra:
ret = b_init();
if (ret)
        goto err_a;
return 0;
err_a:
        a_exit();

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.text: Kernel return conventions: actions return {{c1::0 on success, a negative errno on failure}}; predicates return {{c2::non-zero/true for "yes"}}; read()/write() handlers return {{c3::a byte count ≥ 0 or a negative errno}}; interrupt request (IRQ) handlers return {{c4::IRQ_HANDLED or IRQ_NONE}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What happens to a kernel negative errno at the system-call boundary?
notes.back: libc turns it into a -1 return with errno set. Propagate the error code you received rather than inventing a new one.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Rewrite val = (reg >> 4) & 0x7; with kernel bitfield helpers.
notes.back:
#define CTRL_MODE GENMASK(6, 4)
val = FIELD_GET(CTRL_MODE, reg);

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Why are GENMASK()/FIELD_PREP()/FIELD_GET() safer than hand-written shifts and masks?
notes.back: One definition per field, matching the datasheet; the shift is derived from the mask at compile time (no separate _SHIFT to drift), GENMASK rejects h < l, and FIELD_PREP rejects constants that don't fit.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What does __attribute__((cleanup(fn))) do?
notes.back: Calls fn(&var) automatically when the variable goes out of scope: scope-based resource management in C.
notes.analogy: Go's defer or a C++ RAII destructor, bolted onto a C variable.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How are the kernel's __free() and guard() (6.5+) used?
notes.back: struct foo *f __free(kfree) = kzalloc(...); frees on every return path; guard(mutex)(&lock); unlocks on every return path; return_ptr(f) hands ownership out without freeing.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What rules apply to kernel scope-based cleanup?
notes.back: Declare and initialise the variable in the same statement, and don't mix it with goto-based unwinding in the same function.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: In a driver, why prefer dev_err(dev, ...) over pr_err()?
notes.back: It prefixes the driver and device name, so the message says which instance failed.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What is pr_fmt for?
notes.back: Defined before the includes (e.g. KBUILD_MODNAME ": " fmt), it prefixes every pr_*() message in the file.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How can dev_dbg()/pr_debug() output be turned on?
notes.back: At runtime per call site with CONFIG_DYNAMIC_DEBUG; otherwise they compile to nothing unless DEBUG is defined.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: printk %p vs %px?
notes.back: %p prints a hashed value so kernel addresses don't leak; %px prints the real address and is for debugging only.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How should a driver log in hot or interrupt paths?
notes.back: With *_ratelimited() or *_once() variants, so a misbehaving device can't flood the log.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How does the kernel kref pattern manage an object's lifetime?
notes.back: kref_init() sets the count to 1, kref_get() increments, and kref_put(&f->ref, release) calls the release callback at zero, which frees the containing struct via container_of().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Why is the kref release function a callback?
notes.back: Whoever drops the last reference frees the object: remove(), the final close() or a work item. That's how state outlives a hot-unplugged device while a file is still open.
notes.analogy: The last person to leave turns off the lights, whoever that turns out to be.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What rules apply when taking kref references?
notes.back: Take a reference before handing the pointer to another context. For lookups use kref_get_unless_zero() under the lookup lock, never kref_get() on a count that may already be zero.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: BUG_ON() vs WARN_ON(): which should a driver use?
notes.back: WARN_ON(): prints a backtrace, taints, continues, and returns the condition so you can recover: if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!x)) return -EINVAL;. BUG_ON() kills the context with locks held; essentially banned in new code.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Why must a WARN_ON() never be triggerable from user space?
notes.back: Systems running with panic_on_warn would reboot, handing user space a denial of service. Expected failures return an errno instead.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Which kernel function copies strings safely, and what does it return?
notes.back: strscpy(dst, src, size): always NUL-terminates; returns the length or -E2BIG on truncation. strcpy, strncpy (for strings) and strlcpy are deprecated or removed.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How should kernel code parse integers from strings?
