notes.back: kstrtoint(), kstrtou32()...: strict, overflow-checked, returning an errno. simple_strtoul() and sscanf() are discouraged.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: snprintf() vs scnprintf() return values?
notes.back: snprintf returns what it would have written; scnprintf what it actually wrote, so it is safe for accumulating offsets. In sysfs show() use sysfs_emit().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Why does kernel style write p = kmalloc(sizeof(*p), GFP_KERNEL);?
notes.back: sizeof(*p) follows p's declared type, so it can't go stale like sizeof(struct foo), and it doesn't evaluate p. No cast: void * converts implicitly and a cast can hide errors.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: Why prefer kzalloc() over kmalloc() by default?
notes.back: Zeroed memory avoids uninitialised-member bugs and information leaks, unless every byte is about to be overwritten anyway.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: An oops reads "NULL pointer dereference at 0000000000000018". What does 0x18 tell you?
notes.back: Code accessed a member at offset 0x18 through a NULL struct pointer. Find the struct in that function with a member at offset 24 (pahole -C struct_name).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: How do you map an oops line RIP: foo_read+0x3c/0x120 [foo] to a source line?
notes.back: scripts/faddr2line foo.ko foo_read+0x3c (needs debug info), or gdb foo.ko with list *(foo_read+0x3c). scripts/decode_stacktrace.sh decodes a whole log.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.text: Kernel run-time checkers: {{c1::KASAN}} finds out-of-bounds access and use-after-free; {{c2::UBSAN}} undefined behaviour such as bad shifts and overflow; {{c3::KMSAN}} use of uninitialised memory; {{c4::KCSAN}} data races.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.text: More kernel checkers: {{c1::kmemleak}} reports unreferenced allocations; {{c2::KFENCE}} is a low-overhead sampling heap checker suitable for production; {{c3::lockdep}} checks lock ordering and context misuse.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Which macros make up a minimal loadable kernel module?
notes.back: module_init(fn)/module_exit(fn) (entry points for insmod/rmmod), __init/__exit section markers, and MODULE_LICENSE("GPL"), which governs access to GNU General Public License (GPL)-only symbols and tainting.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: How is an out-of-tree module built?
notes.back: Makefile obj-m += foo.o, then make -C /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build M=$PWD modules: always against the exact configured kernel it will load into, or vermagic/symbol versions mismatch.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why do real drivers rarely write module_init()/module_exit() by hand?
notes.back: Helpers such as module_platform_driver() generate them, registering and unregistering the driver struct.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.text: Character device setup: {{c1::alloc_chrdev_region()}} reserves a major/minor; {{c2::cdev_init() + cdev_add()}} binds it to the file_operations; {{c3::class_create() + device_create()}} creates sysfs entries so udev/devtmpfs makes /dev/foo.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is the shortcut for exposing a single /dev node?
notes.back: struct miscdevice with misc_register(): major 10, dynamic minor, node created automatically.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: In a character device's open(), how do you get the driver state?
notes.back: container_of(inode->i_cdev, struct foo, cdev), then store it in file->private_data for the other file operations.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does a character device read handler return?
notes.back: The number of bytes transferred (may be less than count), 0 for end of file, or a negative errno. Copy with copy_to_user() (→ -EFAULT on failure).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why does cat /dev/foo loop forever on some drivers?
notes.back: Their read() always returns count and never 0 (EOF). Advance *ppos and return 0 at the end; simple_read_from_buffer() does this for a memory buffer.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What should a read() handler do when no data is available?
notes.back: Block with wait_event_interruptible(), or return -EAGAIN if file->f_flags & O_NONBLOCK.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does an ioctl number built with _IOR('f', 1, struct foo_status) encode?
notes.back: In 32 bits: direction (from user space's point of view), argument size, a magic/type byte and a sequence number.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: How do you design an ioctl argument struct that works for 32-bit user space on a 64-bit kernel?
notes.back: Fixed-width __u32/__u64 only: no long, pointers (pass as __u64), enums or bitfields; explicit padding with 64-bit members 8-aligned; reserved-must-be-zero fields and a flags word for extension.
notes.extra: Then .compat_ioctl = compat_ptr_ioctl suffices.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What should an ioctl handler return for an unknown command, and how should it treat its argument?
notes.back: -ENOTTY. Copy the argument into kernel memory once, validate it, then act on the copy.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.text: Linux device model: a bus {{c1::enumerates devices and matches them to drivers}}; a device (struct device) represents {{c2::one hardware instance}}; a driver registers {{c3::a match table and callbacks}}.
notes.analogy: The bus is a dating agency: it knows the devices and each driver's match criteria, and introduces matching pairs (probe).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: When does the driver core call probe() and remove()?
notes.back: probe() when a device and driver on the same bus match (Peripheral Component Interconnect (PCI)/USB IDs, device tree (DT) compatible, Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) ID, name). remove() on unbind, module unload or hot-unplug.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why must driver state live in a struct allocated in probe() rather than in globals?
notes.back: There may be several instances of the device; each probe() call needs its own state.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(of, foo_of_match) do?
notes.back: Exports the match table as module aliases so udev can autoload the module when a matching device appears.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: In a Device Tree platform driver's probe(), how do you map the registers and get the interrupt request (IRQ)?
notes.back: regs = devm_platform_ioremap_resource(pdev, 0); (check IS_ERR) and irq = platform_get_irq(pdev, 0); (negative means error).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: How does a platform driver declare which Device Tree nodes it binds to?
notes.back: An of_device_id table with .compatible = "acme,foo-1.0", referenced from .driver.of_match_table, registered with module_platform_driver().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why does a platform driver call platform_set_drvdata(pdev, foo)?
notes.back: So remove(), power management (PM) callbacks and others can retrieve the per-device state with platform_get_drvdata().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is the Device Tree?
notes.back: A data structure describing non-discoverable hardware (system on chip (SoC) peripherals, Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C)/Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) devices). .dts is compiled by dtc into a .dtb that the bootloader passes to the kernel, so one kernel binary serves many boards.
notes.analogy: A floor plan handed to the electrician on arrival: the same electrician (kernel) can work in any building that comes with a plan.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: How does a driver read a custom Device Tree property in a firmware-agnostic way?
notes.back: device_property_read_u32(dev, "acme,fifo-depth", &depth), which also works with Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What belongs in the Device Tree, and what doesn't?
notes.back: Hardware description only (reg, interrupts, clocks), not policy or Linux configuration. Custom properties get a vendor prefix and a YAML binding schema.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What are devm_* managed resources?
notes.back: Resources (memory, ioremap, interrupt requests (IRQs), clocks) tied to the device binding and released automatically, in reverse order, when probe() fails or after remove(). Most goto unwinding disappears.
notes.analogy: Hotel charges billed to the room: checkout (unbind) settles them all automatically, in reverse order.
notes.extra: Only for probe()-time resources, not per-open() or per-request allocations.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is the classic devm lifetime bug with open files?
notes.back: devm memory is freed at unbind, but user space may still hold an open fd whose file operations dereference it: use-after-free. State reachable from open files needs its own refcount (kref).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why can a devm-requested interrupt request (IRQ) handler still run during remove()?
notes.back: devm frees the IRQ only after remove() returns. Quiesce the hardware first, or free the IRQ explicitly.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why access memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) with readl()/writel() on an __iomem pointer rather than a plain dereference?
notes.back: They guarantee a single access of exactly that width with the required barriers; a plain dereference may be merged, split, reordered or widened. They also port to architectures where MMIO isn't a normal load/store, and sparse checks __iomem.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What byte order do readl()/writel() assume?
notes.back: Little-endian: they byte-swap on big-endian CPUs. Use ioread32be() for big-endian devices.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: A status register has write-1-to-clear bits. What is wrong with writel(readl(STATUS) | IRQ_RX, STATUS);?
notes.back: The read returns all pending bits; writing them back as 1s acknowledges every pending interrupt, including unhandled ones, so events are lost intermittently. Write only the bit to clear: writel(IRQ_RX, regs + STATUS);
notes.analogy: An alarm panel where pressing a lit button silences it: reading every lit alarm and pressing them all silences ones nobody dealt with.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: When is read-modify-write on a device register valid?
notes.back: Only for plain read/write registers. Check every field's access type in the datasheet: write-1-to-clear (W1C), read-to-clear, write-only, self-clearing.
notes.extra: Firmware has the same trap: TIMx->SR |= flag; is wrong.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What must an interrupt request (IRQ) handler on a shared line (IRQF_SHARED) do first?
notes.back: Check whether its own device raised the interrupt and return IRQ_NONE if not; the core uses this to detect and disable stuck "nobody cared" lines.
notes.analogy: Several flats on one doorbell wire: each tenant checks whether the visitor is theirs before answering.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why must a level-triggered interrupt request (IRQ) handler clear the device-side source before returning?
notes.back: Otherwise the line is still asserted and the interrupt fires again immediately.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is the role of dev_id in request_irq()?
notes.back: It is passed to the handler (usually the device struct) and must be unique per device: free_irq() uses it as the key on a shared line.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: When in probe() should a driver request its interrupt request (IRQ)?
notes.back: Only after everything the handler uses is initialised: the interrupt can fire immediately.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What should a hard interrupt request (IRQ) handler (top half) do?
notes.back: Acknowledge the hardware, capture volatile state, and defer everything else.
notes.analogy: A receptionist logs the call and hands the work to a back-office clerk (thread) who can take their time.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is a threaded interrupt, and why is it the default choice for new drivers?
notes.back: request_threaded_irq(irq, hard_fn, thread_fn, IRQF_ONESHOT, ...): thread_fn runs in a kernel thread and may sleep (mutexes, Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C)/Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) transfers). Mandatory for devices behind slow buses.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.text: Deferral mechanisms: {{c1::workqueues}} run in process context and may sleep; {{c2::softirqs}} are a fixed set for core subsystems (network drivers use them via New API (NAPI)); {{c3::tasklets}} run in atomic context and are deprecated.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What must remove() do about deferred work and timers?
notes.back: Cancel them synchronously (cancel_work_sync(), timer_delete_sync()) and free_irq(): nothing may fire after teardown.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Direct memory access (DMA) API: coherent vs streaming mappings?
notes.back: Coherent (dma_alloc_coherent()): long-lived memory both CPU and device may access at any time without syncing, e.g. descriptor rings; possibly uncached. Streaming (dma_map_single()/dma_map_sg()): maps an existing buffer for one transfer, with a direction.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is the ownership rule for a streaming direct memory access (DMA) mapping?
notes.back: Between map and unmap the buffer belongs to the device and the CPU must not touch it; map/unmap do the cache flush/invalidate. To peek without unmapping: dma_sync_single_for_cpu()/_for_device().
notes.analogy: A library book on loan: while the device has it checked out, the CPU may not write in it.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What must you check after dma_map_single()?
notes.back: dma_mapping_error(dev, addr): mapping can fail, e.g. when input-output memory management unit (IOMMU) or bounce-buffer space is exhausted.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Which memory must NOT be used for streaming direct memory access (DMA)?
notes.back: Stack memory, vmalloc memory via dma_map_single(), module globals and .rodata, and small buffers sharing cache lines with fields the CPU keeps using. kmalloc and page-allocator memory are fine.
notes.extra: CONFIG_DMA_API_DEBUG catches most misuse.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does the direct memory access (DMA) mask (dma_set_mask_and_coherent(dev, DMA_BIT_MASK(32))) do?
notes.back: Declares how many address bits the device can drive; buffers beyond that are reached via input-output memory management unit (IOMMU) mappings or swiotlb bounce buffers. Set it in probe() and check the result.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: A driver writes a reset bit, then calls udelay(10); on Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) the device sometimes isn't reset in time. Why?
notes.back: PCIe memory writes are posted: the CPU moves on once the write is queued, so the delay can start before the device sees it. Read back any register of that device (reads are non-posted) to flush it first.
notes.analogy: A posted write is a letter dropped in a mailbox; the read-back is a phone call that can't connect until the earlier letters have arrived.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is better than a fixed delay after resetting a device?
notes.back: Polling a status bit with a timeout: readl_poll_timeout(addr, val, cond, sleep_us, timeout_us) from <linux/iopoll.h>.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.text: Kernel delays: {{c1::udelay()}} busy-waits (the only option in atomic context, a few µs); {{c2::usleep_range(min, max)}} sleeps on an hrtimer (~10 µs to 20 ms); {{c3::msleep()}} is jiffies-based (≥ 20 ms); {{c4::fsleep()}} picks automatically.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why can msleep(1) take 10–20 ms?
notes.back: It is jiffies-based, so its resolution depends on HZ (ticks of several ms) plus rounding up.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What rule applies to every wait on hardware in a driver?
notes.back: It needs a timeout and an error path, because hardware does hang. Prefer an interrupt request (IRQ) plus completion, or readl_poll_timeout(), over fixed delays.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is regmap, and why use it in Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C)/Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) device drivers?
notes.back: A bus-independent register API (regmap_read/write/update_bits()): one driver core for I2C and SPI variants, locked read-modify-write, a register cache (fewer bus transfers, restore after suspend), and debugfs dumps.
notes.analogy: A universal remote: the same buttons whether the TV listens over infrared (I2C) or Bluetooth (SPI), and it remembers the last settings.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why do Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C)/Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) device drivers need threaded interrupt requests (IRQs) and mutexes rather than hard handlers and spinlocks?
notes.back: Bus transfers sleep, so they can't run in hard-IRQ context or under a spinlock.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: How does a driver's mmap handler map device registers into user space?
notes.back: Set vma->vm_page_prot = pgprot_noncached(vma->vm_page_prot), then io_remap_pfn_range(vma, vma->vm_start, phys >> PAGE_SHIFT, size, vma->vm_page_prot).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.text: mmap backends: a coherent direct memory access (DMA) buffer uses {{c1::dma_mmap_coherent()}}; vmalloc memory uses {{c2::remap_vmalloc_range()}}; individual pages use {{c3::vm_insert_page()}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What are the security pitfalls of a driver mmap handler?
notes.back: Not validating offset and size lets user space map arbitrary physical memory. Mappings are page-granular, so the rest of the page is exposed too, and they can outlive close().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does returning -EPROBE_DEFER from probe() mean?
notes.back: A dependency (clock, regulator, general-purpose input/output (GPIO), physical layer transceiver (PHY)...) isn't available yet because its provider hasn't probed; the core retries after other drivers bind.
notes.analogy: A guest who arrives before the host waits in the lobby and is let in once the host shows up.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does dev_err_probe(dev, err, msg) do?
notes.back: Logs the error except for -EPROBE_DEFER (whose reason it records in debugfs devices_deferred instead) and returns err.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does probe deferral imply for how you write probe()?
notes.back: Acquire all resources before touching hardware or registering interfaces, and make probe() safe to run repeatedly.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is the first choice for a driver's user-space interface?
notes.back: An existing subsystem (industrial I/O (IIO), hwmon, input, Video4Linux 2 (V4L2), netdev, tty, general-purpose input/output (GPIO)), for which user space already has tools, rather than a custom character device.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.text: Driver interfaces: {{c1::sysfs}} for simple config/state, one text value per file, stable; {{c2::ioctl}} for structured commands and binary data; {{c3::debugfs}} for debugging only, with no stability promise; {{c4::netlink}} for async events and complex config, mainly networking.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why design every user-facing driver interface for extension from day one?
notes.back: Once exposed it must never break; flags words and reserved fields leave room to grow.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What stability does Linux promise for the in-kernel driver API vs the user-space application binary interface (ABI)?
notes.back: In-kernel API/ABI: none; signatures and structs change every release (stable-api-nonsense.rst). User-space ABI (syscalls, ioctls, sysfs): stable indefinitely; "we do not break user space".

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What is the practical consequence for embedded products with out-of-tree drivers?
notes.back: Upstream the driver or budget to forward-port it at every kernel upgrade. Vendor board support package (BSP) kernels full of out-of-tree drivers are why devices stay on old, unpatched kernels.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: When is a user-space driver (userspace I/O (UIO), spidev, i2c-dev, libgpiod, virtual function I/O (VFIO)) appropriate?
notes.back: Simple or one-off devices, modest latency needs, nothing else in the kernel depends on it, or the logic is proprietary or needs floating point. Crashes don't take the kernel down and there is no dependence on the in-kernel API.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: When is a user-space driver NOT suitable?
notes.back: When the device is needed during boot, other drivers depend on it (clocks, regulators), a standard interface is expected, interrupt latency is critical, or direct memory access (DMA) is needed without an input-output memory management unit (IOMMU).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What does VFIO enable?
notes.back: Safe, direct memory access (DMA)-capable device access from user space, isolated by the input-output memory management unit (IOMMU); used by DPDK/SPDK and for passing devices through to VMs.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Runtime power management (PM): what pattern must surround every hardware access?
notes.back: pm_runtime_resume_and_get(dev) before (fail if < 0), then pm_runtime_mark_last_busy() and pm_runtime_put_autosuspend() after. Touching a block whose clock or power domain is off gives a bus error or a hang.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why prefer pm_runtime_resume_and_get() over pm_runtime_get_sync()?
notes.back: It drops its usage reference on failure; get_sync doesn't, so error paths leak a reference unless you put it manually.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What do the runtime_suspend/runtime_resume callbacks do, and how is runtime power management (PM) switched on?
notes.back: Gate/ungate clocks and save/restore register context. pm_runtime_enable() in probe(), pm_runtime_disable() in remove().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What is the standard bare-metal C idiom for a single memory-mapped register?
notes.back: #define REG (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40023830u): volatile makes every access a real bus access, uint32_t fixes the width, the u suffix keeps the constant unsigned.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: How do CMSIS-style headers model a peripheral's registers?
notes.back: A struct of volatile uint32_t members at the right offsets (with explicit reserved gaps), overlaid on the base address: #define USART1 ((USART_TypeDef *)0x40011000u).
notes.extra: Verify offsets with static_assert(offsetof(...)).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What happens to while (!(USART1->SR & TXE)); if the register isn't declared volatile?
notes.back: The compiler may load SR once and spin forever on the cached value.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: GPIOA->ODR |= 1u << 5; runs in main() while an interrupt service routine (ISR) also changes GPIOA pins. What is the bug?
notes.back: |= is load, OR, store. An ISR between the load and the store has its change undone by the stale write-back: rare and very hard to reproduce.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Which hardware features avoid read-modify-write races on general-purpose input/output (GPIO) outputs?
notes.back: Set/clear registers where only written 1-bits take effect (STM32 BSRR, others OUTSET/OUTCLR), or Cortex-M3/M4 bit-banding; otherwise a critical section.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What does Cortex-M hardware push on exception entry?
notes.back: r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR (plus FP registers if that context is active) onto the current stack, then loads an EXC_RETURN value into lr.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why can a Cortex-M interrupt service routine (ISR) be a plain void f(void) C function?
notes.back: The hardware-pushed set is exactly the Arm Architecture Procedure Call Standard (AAPCS) caller-saved registers, and an ordinary bx lr to EXC_RETURN triggers unstacking. No assembly wrapper or interrupt attribute needed (unlike classic ARM, reduced instruction set computer (RISC)-V, AVR).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.text: Cortex-M {{c1::tail-chaining}} lets back-to-back interrupts skip the pop/push pair; {{c2::late arrival}} services a higher-priority interrupt request (IRQ) that arrives during stacking first.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: In the Cortex-M nested vectored interrupt controller (NVIC), does a lower priority number mean higher or lower priority?
notes.back: Higher. Only the top N bits of the 8-bit field are implemented (often 3 or 4); NVIC_SetPriority() shifts for you, and writing raw unshifted values is a classic bug.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: PRIMASK vs BASEPRI on Cortex-M?
notes.back: PRIMASK (__disable_irq()) masks everything except non-maskable interrupt (NMI) and HardFault. BASEPRI (ARMv7-M and later, not M0) masks only priorities at or below a threshold, so critical high-priority interrupt requests (IRQs) keep running.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: How does FreeRTOS use BASEPRI, and what is the rule for very high-priority interrupt service routines (ISRs)?
notes.back: Its critical sections mask only up to configMAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY. ISRs above it (numerically lower) are never masked by the kernel, but must not call any FreeRTOS API.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What are the core design rules for a firmware interrupt service routine (ISR)?
notes.back: Short and bounded: acknowledge, move data, set a flag or notify a task, return. No blocking, delays, printf(), malloc() or non-reentrant calls.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why should an interrupt service routine (ISR) clear its interrupt source early rather than as its last instruction?
notes.back: A clearing write at the very end may not have propagated through the bus before exception return, causing a spurious second entry. Clear early, or read back / __DSB().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why does the worst-case run time of one interrupt service routine (ISR) matter to other, unrelated interrupts?
notes.back: It adds directly to the latency of every lower-priority interrupt.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Cortex-M HardFault: which stacked value identifies the faulting instruction, and how do you find it?
notes.back: The stacked pc. Bit 2 of EXC_RETURN in lr says whether main stack pointer (MSP) or process stack pointer (PSP) was active; read the frame from that stack and look up the pc with addr2line or the map file.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Which registers explain the cause of a Cortex-M fault?
notes.back: CFSR (configurable fault status), HFSR, and the fault addresses in MMFAR/BFAR when their valid bits are set.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What are common causes of a Cortex-M HardFault?
notes.back: NULL or wild pointers, a peripheral with its clock off, stack overflow, calling a function pointer without the Thumb bit (INVSTATE), trapped unaligned access or divide by zero, returning from a real-time operating system (RTOS) task.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What does IMPRECISERR mean in a Cortex-M fault?
notes.back: The bus fault was reported late (buffered write), so the stacked pc is unreliable. Temporarily disable write buffering (DISDEFWBUF) to make it precise.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: How does a stack overflow show up on a microcontroller without a memory management unit (MMU)?
notes.back: Silently: the stack grows into .bss, the heap or another task's stack, and symptoms (globals changing, faults in unrelated code) appear far from the cause.
notes.analogy: A car park with no barrier at the end: overflowing cars quietly roll into the neighbour's garden.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: How can you detect stack overflow on a microcontroller?
notes.back: -fstack-usage analysis, stack painting with high-water marks, FreeRTOS configCHECK_FOR_STACK_OVERFLOW, a memory protection unit (MPU) guard region, or ARMv8-M MSPLIM/PSPLIM limit registers.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why place a microcontroller unit (MCU)'s main stack at the bottom of RAM?
notes.back: It grows downward, so an overflow runs off the start of RAM into unmapped space and faults immediately instead of corrupting data.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why must Cortex-M stack budgets include interrupts?
notes.back: All handlers run on the main stack, nested, on top of whatever is already there.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why is dynamic memory allocation avoided in small embedded systems?
notes.back: Fragmentation over months of uptime in a few KiB of RAM, non-deterministic timing, no sensible reaction to NULL deep in a control loop, and leaks are fatal in a device that never restarts.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What replaces malloc() in small embedded systems?
notes.back: Static allocation sized for the worst case (the linker proves it fits), allocate-once at init, fixed-block memory pools (O(1), no fragmentation), FreeRTOS static allocation.
notes.analogy: Fixed-block pools are egg cartons: every slot holds exactly one egg, so odd-shaped gaps never appear.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What is a watchdog timer for?
notes.back: An independent hardware counter that resets the system unless software refreshes it in time: the last line of defence against hangs, deadlocks and runaway code.
notes.analogy: A dead man's switch: the train stops unless the driver keeps proving they are awake.
notes.extra: Cloud analogue: a Kubernetes liveness probe restarting an unresponsive container.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why not refresh a watchdog from a timer interrupt?
notes.back: Interrupts keep running while the main loop is dead, so the watchdog would never fire. Refresh from the main loop or a supervisor task, only after every critical task has checked in.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What does a windowed watchdog add?
notes.back: It also resets if refreshed too early, catching code stuck in a tight loop around the refresh call.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What should firmware do with the reset cause after boot?
notes.back: Read and log the reset-cause register; an unnoticed watchdog reset hides a bug.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: A new peripheral driver reads zeros from every register and its writes have no effect. Most likely cause?
notes.back: The peripheral's clock is gated off (or it is held in reset / its power domain is down): most microcontroller unit (MCU) peripherals are unclocked after reset. Enable its clock first, plus the general-purpose input/output (GPIO) port clock and pin alternate function.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What is the Linux equivalent of "enable the peripheral clock first"?
notes.back: devm_clk_get_enabled(), the reset-controller API and runtime power management (PM) in probe(). Forgetting them gives a synchronous external abort on the first readl().

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: On a Cortex-M7 with a data cache, why is direct memory access (DMA) data sometimes stale or wrong?
notes.back: The DMA engine uses RAM while the CPU sees its cache. Before TX, clean (flush) the buffer to RAM; after RX, invalidate the range before reading.
notes.extra: Linux's dma_map_single()/dma_sync_*() do exactly this; on bare metal it is your job.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why must direct memory access (DMA) buffers on a cached microcontroller unit (MCU) be cache-line aligned and padded?
notes.back: Cache maintenance works on whole lines (32 B on Cortex-M7); if a line is shared, invalidating it corrupts neighbouring variables. Alternative: a memory protection unit (MPU)-marked non-cacheable region.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Microcontroller vs application processor: what are the key software-visible differences?
notes.back: Microcontroller unit (MCU) (Cortex-M): no memory management unit (MMU), KiB–MiB of on-chip memory, execute-in-place flash, deterministic interrupt latency; runs bare metal or a real-time operating system (RTOS). Application processor (Cortex-A, x86): MMU, dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), caches, multicore; runs Linux with virtual memory and isolation.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What common system on chip (SoC) architecture combines both kinds of core?
notes.back: Linux on application cores for connectivity and UI, plus a microcontroller core for hard real-time control, talking over RPMsg or shared memory.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.text: Embedded Linux boot chain: {{c1::Boot ROM}} (loads the first stage, verifies secure boot) → {{c2::SPL / first-stage loader}} (initialises dynamic random-access memory (DRAM)) → {{c3::U-Boot}} (loads kernel, device tree blob (DTB) and initramfs; sets bootargs) → {{c4::Linux kernel}} → init.
notes.analogy: A relay race where each runner is only strong enough to carry the next, bigger runner to the start line.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why does the embedded boot chain need a secondary program loader (SPL) before U-Boot?
notes.back: At reset only on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM) is usable; the SPL is small enough to fit there and initialises the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) controller so the full bootloader can be loaded into DRAM.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: How are robust field updates of embedded Linux usually done?
notes.back: A/B partitions with a boot counter and automatic rollback.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Super-loop vs real-time operating system (RTOS): what are the trade-offs?
notes.back: Super-loop: simple, one stack, but any function's worst-case response is the sum of all the others. RTOS: preemptive priority tasks and blocking calls, at the cost of RAM per stack plus races, deadlock and priority inversion.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: In FreeRTOS, how does an interrupt service routine (ISR) hand work to a task?
notes.back: xQueueSendFromISR(q, &c, &woken), then portYIELD_FROM_ISR(woken) to switch immediately if a higher-priority task woke; the task blocks in xQueueReceive().
notes.extra: Same split as top half / threaded handler in Linux.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Low-power loop if (!event_flag) __WFI();: what is the race, and the correct Cortex-M idiom?
notes.back: If the interrupt request (IRQ) fires after the test but before wait for interrupt (WFI), the core sleeps with the flag set: a lost wake-up. Fix: __disable_irq(); if (!flag) __WFI(); __enable_irq();. WFI still wakes on a pending IRQ with PRIMASK set, so there's no window.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What must a Cortex-M bootloader do to jump to an application?
notes.back: Validate the image; disable interrupt requests (IRQs), stop SysTick and the peripherals/direct memory access (DMA) it used, clear pending IRQs; set SCB->VTOR to the app base; load main stack pointer (MSP) from the app's word 0; jump to the reset handler in word 1.
notes.extra: The application must be linked for that base address.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why must a bootloader de-initialise its peripherals before jumping to the application?
notes.back: Peripherals left running with interrupts enabled will fire into the application's handlers before it is ready.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What must the jump code avoid after __set_MSP()?
notes.back: Touching stack-based locals, because the stack pointer just moved. Production code does the last steps in assembly or a naked function.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: On Cortex-M, why declare lookup tables static const?
notes.back: Static const data goes to .rodata in flash and uses no RAM; without const it lands in .data: a flash copy plus RAM.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: const char *names[] vs const char *const names[] on a microcontroller?
notes.back: The first is a writable array of pointers, so it lives in RAM; only the second lives entirely in flash.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What is special about const data on a classic 8-bit AVR?
notes.back: Harvard architecture: normal pointers can't address flash, so const data is copied to RAM at start-up unless you use PROGMEM + pgm_read_byte() or __flash.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What is MISRA C?
notes.back: Motor Industry Software Reliability Association guidelines restricting C to a subset that avoids undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour, for safety-related systems; checked by static analysers, with documented deviations.
notes.analogy: Building codes for C: they forbid constructions known to collapse, whatever the builder's skill.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.text: MISRA C examples: Rule 17.2 {{c1::no recursion (bounded stack)}}; Rule 21.3 / Directive 4.12 {{c2::no dynamic memory}}; Rule 13.2 {{c3::no dependence on evaluation order}}; Rules 10.x {{c4::no implicit conversions that change signedness or narrow}}.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Which standards require a coding standard such as MISRA, and does Linux follow MISRA?
notes.back: Functional-safety standards such as IEC 61508 and ISO 26262 (CERT C is the security-oriented counterpart). The Linux kernel does not follow MISRA.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.text: Cortex-M debug: {{c1::SWD/JTAG}} gives halt, step, hardware breakpoints and data watchpoints; {{c2::ITM over SWO}} gives cheap printf-style output; {{c3::RTT}} uses a RAM ring buffer read by the probe, fast enough for interrupt service routines (ISRs); {{c4::semihosting}} runs printf on the host, very slow and hangs without a debugger.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What is the best tool for finding who corrupts a memory location in firmware?
notes.back: A data watchpoint (a data watchpoint and trace (DWT) comparator) via serial wire debug (SWD)/Joint Test Action Group (JTAG): the core halts on the offending write.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: How do you capture firmware field failures without a debugger attached?
notes.back: Store the fault registers and stacked frame in no-init RAM or flash, and report them after the reboot.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What is the most accurate way to measure firmware timing?
notes.back: Toggle a general-purpose input/output (GPIO) and watch it on an oscilloscope or logic analyser (or read the data watchpoint and trace (DWT) cycle counter).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: A checked access if (idx < len) use(a[idx]) uses signed int idx. What input defeats it, and what is the fix?
notes.back: A negative idx passes idx < len (or a signed/unsigned comparison converts it to a huge value). Make the index unsigned or check idx >= 0 explicitly, and build with -Wsign-compare.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: Why does the optimiser deleting an overflow check not count as a compiler bug?
notes.back: The check relies on undefined behaviour (UB). The standard lets the compiler assume UB never happens, so code that can only be true after UB is dead. The bug is in the source: test before the operation instead.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::01 Undefined Behaviour & Integers
notes.front: What does a wrapping millis() timeout like (uint32_t)(now - start) >= timeout need to stay correct, and what breaks it?
notes.back: Unsigned subtraction, modulo 232, gives the true elapsed time across a wrap, provided the real interval is under 231 ticks. Comparing absolute timestamps (now >= start + timeout) fails at the wrap.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: Why can a const T * parameter not be used by the compiler to cache the data across a call to unknown code?
notes.back: const only restricts writes through that pointer. Another alias, an interrupt service routine (ISR) or another thread may still change the data, so the compiler must reload it. Only restrict adds the no-alias promise.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::02 Pointers, Qualifiers & Declarations
notes.front: A driver passes the address of a local buffer to a direct memory access (DMA) engine and returns before the transfer ends. What happens, and what is the fix?
notes.back: The stack frame is reused, so the device writes into whatever lives there now: random stack corruption. Use a buffer that outlives the transfer (heap or device state allocated in probe()) and wait for completion before freeing.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: Why does reordering struct members change what a driver sends over a wire or to hardware, and how do you guard against it?
notes.back: The compiler inserts padding to satisfy alignment, so layout depends on member order and the application binary interface (ABI). Hardware or wire formats fix exact offsets; pin them with static_assert(offsetof(...) == N) and sizeof checks, or use explicit reserved fields.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: A driver copies a stack struct to user space with every named member assigned. What can still leak, and why does it matter?
notes.back: Padding bytes (and any unassigned member) keep stale kernel stack data, so user space can read kernel pointers or secrets. That defeats kernel address space layout randomization (KASLR). Zero the whole struct with memset() before filling it.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::03 Memory Layout & ABI
notes.front: You read a 32-bit little-endian field from a received packet buffer on a big-endian CPU, using *(u32 *)p. Name every way this can be wrong.
notes.back: It may be unaligned (fault on strict-alignment CPUs), it violates strict aliasing, and it ignores byte order (value byte-swapped). Use get_unaligned_le32(p), which fixes alignment and endianness at once.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: What goes wrong if a Cortex-M startup file skips copying .data from flash to RAM, but zeroes .bss?
notes.back: Initialised globals read as garbage or zero in RAM instead of their declared values (the initial values still sit unused in flash), while uninitialised globals look fine. Bugs appear only in code touching initialised globals, which makes them hard to spot.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: Why does a missing volatile only show up when you raise the optimisation level?
notes.back: At -O0 every variable access goes to memory. At -O2 the compiler may keep a value in a register, hoist a load out of a loop, or delete a loop with no visible side effect. volatile forbids exactly those optimisations.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::04 Toolchain, Linking & Startup
notes.front: A driver module loads, but calling it prints "Unknown symbol in module". Where is the problem and what are the two fixes?
notes.back: The module uses a kernel function that is not exported to modules (or is exported only with EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL while the module declares a non-GNU General Public License (GPL)-compatible license). Fix: use a properly exported API, or change the license/export on the kernel side.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why does spin_lock() in process context deadlock if the same lock is also taken in a hard interrupt handler, and what is the fix?
notes.back: The interrupt can fire on the same CPU while the lock is held, and the handler spins forever on a lock its own CPU owns. Use spin_lock_irqsave() in process context so local interrupts are off while the lock is held.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What breaks if a driver calls mutex_lock() from an interrupt request (IRQ) handler?
notes.back: Mutexes may sleep, but a hard IRQ handler has no process context to put to sleep: the kernel reports "scheduling while atomic" or deadlocks. Use a spinlock there, or move the work to a threaded handler or workqueue.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: What breaks if a Cortex-M critical section ends with __enable_irq() instead of restoring the saved PRIMASK?
notes.back: If the section was entered with interrupts already disabled (nested critical section, or called from an interrupt service routine (ISR)), it re-enables them too early, so the outer section is no longer protected. Save and restore the previous state.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: In a single-producer single-consumer ring buffer, what bug appears if the producer advances head before writing the data?
notes.back: The consumer sees the new index and reads a slot whose data has not been written yet, getting stale or garbage bytes. Write the data first, then publish the index (with a barrier on multicore).

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::05 Concurrency & Interrupt Context
notes.front: Why is a refcount a better tool than a lock for keeping an object alive while another context uses it?
notes.back: A lock only protects access during the critical section, not the object after you release it. A reference count (kref) keeps the object allocated until the last user drops it, so the pointer stays valid across sleeps and context hand-offs.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What goes wrong if you call kfree(p) on a pointer that holds an ERR_PTR() value?
notes.back: The value is a small negative errno disguised as an address, not a heap pointer, so the allocator crashes or corrupts memory. Check IS_ERR(p) first and propagate PTR_ERR(p) instead of freeing.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: A probe() acquires A, B, C in order, and C fails. Which labels run, and what bug appears if the unwind order is not reversed?
notes.back: Only the cleanup for B then A runs, in reverse order of acquisition. Releasing in another order can free a resource that a later one still depends on (for example freeing memory before the interrupt that uses it), giving use-after-free or leaks.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: What goes wrong if you use list_for_each_entry() (not the _safe form) and call list_del() plus kfree() inside the loop?
notes.back: The iterator reads pos->member.next after the body to advance, but pos is freed and its pointers poisoned: use-after-free or a poison-address fault. The _safe variant saves the next entry first.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::06 Kernel C Idioms
notes.front: When is a WARN_ON() the wrong tool and an error return the right one?
notes.back: When the condition can be triggered by user input or by a misbehaving device. Warnings can reboot machines running with panic_on_warn and flood logs. Reserve WARN_ON() for conditions that indicate a kernel bug.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What goes wrong if a driver registers its interrupt handler with request_irq() before initialising the data the handler uses?
notes.back: The interrupt may fire immediately, so the handler dereferences uninitialised state (NULL pointer, uninitialised lock). Request the interrupt last in probe(), after all state is ready.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What breaks if a shared-line interrupt handler always returns IRQ_HANDLED, even when its device did not raise the interrupt?
notes.back: The kernel cannot tell a spurious interrupt from a real one, so other devices on the line may lose their interrupts and a stuck line is never detected and disabled. Return IRQ_NONE when your device status shows nothing pending.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What breaks if you omit dma_sync_single_for_cpu() before the CPU reads a streaming direct memory access (DMA) receive buffer?
notes.back: On a non-coherent system the CPU cache may hold stale lines from before the transfer, so the CPU reads old data instead of what the device wrote. Sync (invalidate) gives the CPU ownership and a fresh view.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why must a driver call dma_mapping_error() instead of assuming a mapping address is valid?
notes.back: Mapping can fail (input-output memory management unit (IOMMU) space or bounce buffers exhausted). Programming the device with an invalid address makes it write to a random location in memory.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: What goes wrong if remove() frees the driver state while a work item or timer is still pending?
notes.back: The deferred callback later runs on freed memory: use-after-free. In remove(), stop the source (interrupt, hardware), cancel work and timers synchronously, then free.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: A probe() returns -EPROBE_DEFER after registering a character device. What is the problem?
notes.back: The core will call probe() again, so the half-finished registration is repeated or leaked, and user space sees a device that does not work. Obtain all dependencies first and register interfaces only once nothing can defer.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::07 Linux Driver Programming
notes.front: Why does a copy_to_user() of a whole kernel struct in an ioctl handler need the struct to be zeroed first?
notes.back: Uninitialised members and padding contain stale kernel memory, which user space then reads (information leak). Use kzalloc() or memset() before filling in the fields.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: A new Cortex-M peripheral reads back zeros and ignores writes, but the code matches the datasheet. What is the first thing to check, and why?
notes.back: Whether its bus clock is enabled (and it is out of reset) in the clock-control registers. A gated peripheral does not respond on the bus, so registers read as zero and writes are dropped.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why is writing a GPIO output with BSRR safe against an interrupt, while ODR |= bit is not?
notes.back: |= is load, OR, store, so an interrupt in between can change other pins and have its change overwritten. BSRR is a single write where only 1-bits act, so no read is needed and other pins are untouched.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What happens if a Cortex-M interrupt handler needs more stack than budgeted?
notes.back: All handlers run on the main stack on top of the interrupted code, and nested interrupts add more. The overflow silently corrupts RAM below the stack (often .bss or the heap), so symptoms look unrelated to the stack.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why does a watchdog refreshed from a timer interrupt fail to protect against a hung main loop?
notes.back: The timer interrupt keeps running while the main loop is stuck, so the watchdog is fed forever. Feed it from the main loop or a supervisor task after confirming that all critical tasks made progress.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: What breaks if a microcontroller bootloader jumps to the application without disabling interrupts and stopping its peripherals?
notes.back: Pending or running peripherals raise interrupts that vector into the application handler table before the application has set it up, causing a fault or erratic behaviour. Quiesce hardware, clear pending interrupts and then set the vector table and stack pointer.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: Why does if (!flag) __WFI(); sometimes sleep forever even though the interrupt fired, and what fixes it?
notes.back: If the interrupt arrives between the test and wait for interrupt (WFI), the flag is set but the core sleeps anyway. Disable interrupts around the check; WFI still wakes on a pending interrupt even while masked, then re-enable.

notes.deck: Deep C: Kernel, Drivers, Embedded::08 Embedded & Bare Metal
notes.front: On a Cortex-M7 with a data cache, which maintenance operation goes before a direct memory access (DMA) transmit and which after a receive, and why?
notes.back: Before transmit, clean (flush) so the DMA reads what the CPU wrote. After receive, invalidate so the CPU reads what the DMA wrote, not stale cache lines. Buffers must be cache-line aligned so maintenance does not affect neighbouring data.
